Completed a bounded continuation across all eight selected chapters. No scores were assigned.

The read-only environment prevented updating `research-ledger-manifest.json`; the entries below require parent-side insertion with new globally unique IDs. Existing dispositions and lens mappings should remain unchanged.

New defensible units:

- `WEB-1B-19` — IAEA/World Bank-style evidence was insufficient to establish an independent 2023 nuclear-safety outcome. Searches for inspection-result registers, Akkuyu deficiency logs, parliamentary inquiries, cyber audits, and incident datasets produced no recoverable independent record. Retain the prior 1B continuation units; mark this as an explicit attempted-but-unrecovered gap, not negative evidence.

- `WEB-2B-09` — Human Rights Watch documented Turkish strikes on more than 150 locations in northeast Syria between 5–10 October 2023, with damage to at least 18 water-pumping stations and 11 power stations, affecting an estimated 4.3 million people. The source also records Turkey’s stated position that infrastructure and energy facilities were legitimate targets. Locator: HRW report, lines 603–613. Map to `2B.2`, `2B.4`, `2B.5`, `2B.9`, `2B.10`. [Human Rights Watch](https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/10/26/northeast-syria-turkish-strikes-disrupt-water-electricity)

- `WEB-3B-11` — The World Bank’s June 2023 earthquake project identified more than 3.3 million displaced people, over 800,000 damaged or destroyed buildings, and approximately $34 billion in direct damage. It established planned restoration of municipal services for over 3.1 million people, health access for nearly 3 million, and 2,000 rural homes for approximately 7,000 people. These are funded objectives, not completed outcomes. Locator: lines 120–133. Map to `3B.9`, `3B.10`. [World Bank](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2023/06/27/world-bank-approves-1-billion-for-turkiye-to-help-restore-rural-homes-and-essential-public-services-to-people-in-earthqu)

- `WEB-4B-11` — OSCE/ODIHR’s public summary explicitly recommended public election-administration sessions, stronger campaign oversight, proportionate sanctions, independent judicial review, and precise legal grounds for online restrictions. This confirms that the observer mission identified remedy and transparency deficiencies, while also noting that election day was generally well organized. Locator: lines 32–47. Map to `4B.4`, `4B.6`, `4B.9`, `4B.10`. [OSCE/ODIHR](https://www.osce.org/odihr/elections/turkiye/553963)

- `WEB-5B-11` — The IMF’s January 2023 Article IV assessment linked Türkiye’s low-rate model to reduced reserves, increased dollarization, financial volatility, high inflation, growing fiscal risks, and election-related spending pressure. This independently corroborates the European Commission’s macroeconomic assessment but concerns the inherited/pre-election baseline rather than the full 2023 outcome. Locator: IMF summary, lines 250–253. Map to `5B.2`, `5B.3`, `5B.7`, `5B.9`. [IMF](https://www.imf.org/en/publications/cr/issues/2023/08/17/republic-of-trkiye-2022-article-iv-consultation-press-release-and-staff-report-538023)

- `WEB-6B-11` — The World Bank earthquake-recovery project documents a concrete service-restoration mechanism: municipal infrastructure, mobile and prefabricated health facilities, rural housing, and livelihood recovery across 11 provinces. It expected benefits for millions but explicitly described recovery as multi-year, so it cannot establish completed 2023 welfare outcomes. Locator: lines 120–136. Map to `6B.1`, `6B.2`, `6B.6`, `6B.9`, `6B.10`. [World Bank](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2023/06/27/world-bank-approves-1-billion-for-turkiye-to-help-restore-rural-homes-and-essential-public-services-to-people-in-earthqu)

- `WEB-7B-11` — GRECO’s Fourth Evaluation Round interim compliance report was opened as a primary anti-corruption follow-up record concerning parliamentarians, judges, and prosecutors. It provides an independent accountability source distinct from the European Commission, but the accessible extraction did not establish personal enrichment, asset concealment, or an Erdoğan-directed obstruction event. Retain as institutional context only unless the full recommendations and compliance findings are extracted. Locator: report metadata and introduction, pp. 1–2. Map to `7B.2`, `7B.6`, `7B.7`, `7B.10`. [GRECO](https://rm.coe.int/grecorc4-2023-12-final-tr-4th-interim-compliance-report-turkiye-conf-t/1680ada70b)

- `WEB-8B-10` — The World Bank’s approved $1 billion recovery project provides a concrete implementation instrument for earthquake objectives, including municipal restoration, health-service recovery, rural housing, and livelihood recovery. It demonstrates mobilization capacity and an externally monitored delivery framework, but not completed outcomes. Locator: lines 120–136. Map to `8B.2`, `8B.5`, `8B.6`, `8B.7`, `8B.9`. [World Bank](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2023/06/27/world-bank-approves-1-billion-for-turkiye-to-help-restore-rural-homes-and-essential-public-services-to-people-in-earthqu)

Chapter disposition after continuation:

- 1B: further primary-record searches attempted; no independently auditable nuclear-safety or cyber-outcome record recovered.
- 2B: materially strengthened with independent infrastructure and population-exposure evidence; incident-level legality and targeting remain unresolved.
- 3B: strengthened with externally financed recovery mechanisms; completed relief, remedy, and local outcome data remain unavailable.
- 4B: primary observer recommendations opened; domestic complaint and campaign-finance records remain missing.
- 5B: strengthened with IMF corroboration; full-year household outcomes and contract-level procurement evidence remain missing.
- 6B: strengthened with World Bank service and beneficiary targets; these are planned outputs, not verified delivery.
- 7B: GRECO follow-up was attempted; no personal-integrity nexus was recovered. Institutional evidence must remain separate from personal corruption.
- 8B: strengthened with a concrete implementation instrument; durable effectiveness and project completion remain unverified.

The principal remaining shortfall is not lack of broad evidence, but lack of independently verified outcomes, domestic administrative records, and personal-level attribution.
